utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Judge Agius will not be with us for the remainder of the week and probably on Monday next week due to an urgent personal matter that he has to attend to. And so as we said yesterday, we'll be sitting -- carry on sitting pursuant to 15 bis. And Mr. Popovic is not with us today as was indicated yesterday with his waiver. I was informed, Mr. Ostojic, that you have a preliminary to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do. Good morning, Your Honours. Two quick points if I may. The first point is that we've consulted with my friends from the office the Prosecution. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, unless there's any opposition from the parties or in particular the Prosecution, there's no reason for the Chamber not to allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next point is our last witness, which will hopefully commence tomorrow sometime. I think his number is 2DW80 if memory serves me correct. We did not file a motion for protective measures. We prepared one late last night. I'm still looking at the draft and hope to get that to the Court today. He lives outside of the former Yugoslavia, and we can explain that to the Court once you receive the motion later this afternoon. But I just wanted everyone to be aware of it. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It may be difficult for the Prosecution to respond without seeing the actual motion, but we'd like to have it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll respond very quickly once we see the motion, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. President, if I may, just -- if I can be given an opportunity to have a 5-minute break after Professor Wagenaar concludes so that we could readjust some of our binders and remove some the documents with respect to the current witness, Professor Wagenaar. Even though it may not be time for the break, we would be asking for that because we have other people who are going to come in instead of our current staff here for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since we are dealing with preliminary matters, there are some matters outstanding with respect to Nikolic Defence. The Chamber is seized of a motion in relation to protective measures with respect to some -- several witnesses, and the Chamber is under advisement and will be issuing the decision in due course. However, I note there's a -- one motion to add one witness on the 65 ter list, and my understanding is that there's no opposition from the Prosecution. The motion was filed, if my memory is correct, on 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe that's no objection, Your Honour, but could I just confirm at the break and...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And also we have two motions regarding the admission of written statements, one pursuant to 92 bis, and the other pursuant to 92 ter. The first one, the former was filed on 20th of August, and the latter on 9th of September. And in particular, the latter one is due to give testimony very soon, so the Chamber likes to hear the Prosecution's position very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Good morning. The 92 bis motion, I believe that's the one -- if I'm thinking of -- we had -- basically a character witness that we had no objection to. The 92 ter motion we will be objecting to and, of course, we'll file something very soon, or we are able to argue it orally, whatever the Chamber prefers. I know Mr. Thayer is working on that as we speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My understanding is he is due to be the first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President. He will be the first witness for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber prefers to have your submissions in writing, and if you could do that by the end of tomorrow or...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No problem. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or during the course of tomorrow so that if necessary, Nikolic Defence team may be able to file a reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That shouldn't be a problem, I know Mr. Thayer is working on it and he -- it shouldn't take long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The 92 bis motion is so granted. And I'm not sure about the degree of urgency, but we also have received a motion regarding a subpoena with respect to one witness and videolink motions with respect to two witnesses, and I also like to have the response from the Prosecution as soon as possible. Yes, let's bring in the witness. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before the witness comes in, I would just like with the leave of the Court simply to clarify something that I said yesterday at page 47, lines 8 to 18, which appears confusing from reading the transcript. At page 47 my colleague said -- sorry, at page 46, lines 20 to 22, yesterday that the Nikolic Defence team had not challenged the encounter between Marko Milosevic and Drago Nikolic. Firstly, it is our position, Mr. President, that this is not entirely correct but more importantly; and secondly, the fact that we ask witness Milosevic to mark where this alleged encounter took place on a map does not mean that we accept nor recognise that Drago Nikolic directed Marko Milosevic to Colonel Beara if that encounter ever took place. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will note it. Mr. Ostojic, for you to continue and conclude your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Re-examination by Mr. Ostojic [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, once again, my sincere appreciation and I thank you for agreeing to come back, and I'm sure we'll get you out of here and back home very shortly. Very much appreciated. Thank you, sir. May I begin?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, yesterday, my learned friend was discussing a category of seven witnesses that I call, actually, witnesses that you've identified as being no identification tests on those witnesses or improper tests that were conducted on those witnesses?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd like to just highlight a couple so that we have at least a clear record, which I'm sure we'll all be more comfortable with. Now, the OTP, the Office of the Prosecution seems to be at least in my view somewhat confused about the issue of retention of names and conducting proper investigations and how they may fall into the mix with wanted posters that we've seen. So let's look at the first witness that we've identified, and that is Mr. Milosevic, which is 126 on our charts respectively that we've identified. And you let me know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to switch off the microphone when the witness is responding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll let me know when you get to that witness, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My first question to you, sir, is when was the first interview conducted with Mr. Milosevic by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I have the date here in my summary notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me try to refresh your memory, Professor. I never gave you that interview. I gave you the testimony that the Court heard when he testified here, but I'll help you. The first interview that the Prosecutor had with Mr. Milosevic was on March 14th, 2002. Now, when my learned friend was asking you that, he simply gave you the year 2002 yesterday, and you seemed to have agreed with him that, yes, if this man gave an interview in 2002 and these wanted posters were actually published in 2002, perhaps an identification test or a photo lineup board would not be necessarily appropriate. And I can give the specific page cite where my friend references that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, I would like the page cite. Just to help my friend, the interview, the 14 March 2002 interview is in the binder which was provided to Professor Wagenaar. That was provided to him. We've copied those binders. We have it as being included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's on page 42, lines 22 through 25, and it proceeds on page 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You agree that first interview was included in the binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I really don't. I don't know. If he says it is, I have no reason to doubt it. I understood that it was not, but it's a minor point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in questioning you if we know as we've established, I think, by looking at these various exhibits that the first wanted poster - and just if you could follow along - was I think on the 30th of October, 2002, then the Interpol one on the 31st of October, 2002. Given that that's approximately six-plus months after this March 14th, 2002, interview, would an identification or a photo board lineup be indicated in a case such as the evidence that was being offered by Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I see in front of me the answer I gave to that question yesterday? Because the way I remembered it is that I said, yes, if the first interrogation was after the publication of those posters, then it would have been improper. I didn't agree that it was improper or that -- and I did not confirm the dates because it's not my business to confirm dates. That's your business. I hope that I said it in that way, if they were published, then. So I would like to see the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I take it that would be sufficient for your answer, but Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it may be difficult providing that answer to the question to the Professor since I never asked him about wanted posters with this witness, and I don't see it in the reference to my friend. Maybe he can help me out. Maybe I'm wrong, but it's 25448 that I'm looking at from yesterday where I start asking questions about Mr. Milosevic, and I don't believe that I ever asked about wanted posters and that the witness didn't answer about wanted posters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So Professor Wagenaar, I don't think it's practically possible for you to see the relevant transcript pages through your monitor, but Mr. Ostojic can read out those parts if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think the professor can answer it straightforward if I'm correct. Let's just add -- let me put another question to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope I may address this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He's put --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you said page 42 of yesterday's transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct. I'll put the question and I'll read it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the page number in the electronic version?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You know, we didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have to add 42 from the first page -- to the first page?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have last night's copy of the transcript, and they don't get updated, the transcripts, from my understanding, until early this morning, so we don't have the paginations that are consistent with the official trial transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the first word that appears on the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On top of the page, the first word that appears is "not". "Not correct, is it..." and then on line 2 the answer was: "No, it should read..." and then it goes on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please read out. The Prosecution can check the accuracy of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As reflected on page 42 of yesterday's transcript, line 22, Prosecution asked the following question, although long so we'll be patient: "Thank you. I want to ask you now about Witness 126, Milosevic. This concerns a 14 July encounter. He's number 10 on your table. He was interviewed in 2002 and testified here in June 2007. This is the witness, you may remember, who was ordered by his commander to deliver a message to Colonel Beara at the school, and he testified at TR1302: 'And later in the day, did you receive some instructions from your commander?' Answer" -- or I'm sorry: "'Answer: Well, yes, sometime in the afternoon he was also called from the brigade, or at least that's what he told me, and he asked me to look for Mr. Beara near the elementary school and to convey a message to him to report to the brigade command, and this is exactly what I did.'" And then Mr. Nicholls proceeds with his next comment and question, I believe. "Now, thinking here about refreshing and names, if you have to deliver a message to someone who you don't know or haven't met named Beara, then you have to remember that name, perhaps even refresh it, as you go along to do the task you were ordered, correct? So the process of imprinting that name Beara would begin even before the encounter?" And then, sir, you provide the following answer on page 43, lines 12 through 14: "Answer: That's one possibility. I'm really not to judge the exact situation. It's also possible that he would be ... go there and there, there is the colonel, and tell him this and that." I'm reading it verbatim. There may be a correction in the transcript from yesterday, but let me put this question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. That's what I was referring to. The first question implied that I'd asked about posters, and only given the date 2002, that's where my difficulty was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this is 25449 of the official transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will follow. Let's hear what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, given that Mr. Milosevic gave an interview on March 14, 2002, and having an appreciation that the wanted posters were first published on October 30th, 2002, was an identification photo board required in this situation?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not for me to state what is required because I'm not aware of any prescriptive rules. My position is that it might have been very helpful to resolve some uncertainties about the testimony of such a witness. About the quote you gave me, that is an example of how I tried constantly to fight the invitation to have to pronounce an opinion about the facts in this case. I think I've been very careful yesterday to constantly emphasize that I'm not to judge the facts. In the quote you gave me, I think I've been very clear to say it's not for me to judge whether someone remembers something or actually whether he has been given a certain name. I can only look at some possibilities. The same applies to the question of dates and publications of posters. It's not for me to determine when interrogations took place, and if you have a question about when interrogations took place, please consult your files. Don't ask me. I'm not an expert on that. The only thing I can state that that's a general principle is that if witnesses have seen pictures of the accused other than at the confrontation that is investigated, then according to my rules - and I think the Prosecution has explained it very carefully and understands it - then it is not useful to apply a photo board identification. If those pictures have seen much later, then, of course, before seeing these pictures it would be very helpful to do a photo board identification. It's a matter of order. But it's not for me to determine in which order the several events took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I got confused because during that same questioning with respect to Mr. Milosevic on the very next page, although counsel was asking you about name retention, he proceeds to tell us the following: "No exposure problem there. This is daylight, two to three" -- I'm sorry, and this was on page 45, lines 1 through 10 of yesterday's transcript. Let me just repeat it. He asked you first about name recognition. Then he goes on to identify the circumstances upon which this purported encounter occurred: "No exposure problem there. This is daylight, 2- to 3-minute conversation, face to face. Is 2- to 3-minute face-to-face conversation adequate? " And sir, you provide the answer "sure", which we have for the record. Now, what does name retention have to do with exposure being proper and the time interval for a face-to-face encounter?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they've got nothing to do with one another, but in many instances, and I've also noted it and even objected against it; I get two or three questions in advance and it gets utterly confused. I don't think that's very helpful. But let me say the following: When -- the question was is two to three minutes sufficient for a perception of a face, which is a general question, I've not been asked to confirm that actually it was two to three minutes or actually this witness saw the face because I cannot know that. The answer to that question definitely should be taken as a general statement about in two to three minutes in principle a person can see a face. It's nothing -- no confirmation of this actual situation because I'm not to judge that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given, Professor, that it seems the Prosecution is conceding that there was adequate exposure time and the parameters of the purported meeting and given that it occurred six months prior to any publication of a wanted poster, can you give me your opinion as to what are the consequences of the Prosecution not conducting a photo board identification lineup of this particular witness?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The consequence is that for the Tribunal it's far more difficult to judge what the reliability of the statement of these witness are. The Tribunal would be very well helped if the Prosecution would have provided such an identification because we know that what we call the diagnostic value, the weight of the evidence, if it is correctly, correctly administered photo identification procedure, the weight of the evidence is high. So depriving the Court of important evidence with a high informational value, I don't think that's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- and I only pause because I'm waiting for the translation to catch up. Thank you. Now, the Prosecution has tried to offer us some explanation as to why they were unable or felt that it was not indicative or indicated to prepare a photo lineup with witnesses that they interviewed purportedly after the 30th of October, 2002. But what I'd like to know is this concept that you introduced yesterday on page 44 on line 6 and 7, and that is reconstruction. You talk about the dangers of reconstruction at that page and line number. Can you share with me first what that is?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you give me more of the context because it means many things. I'd like to be reminded to the exact context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very fair, if I may. It's just a long answer that you actually gave. It starts off, for my learned friends, on page 43, line 20.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe we don't need it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm going to object to the level of argument being introduced to these questions. That question very simply could have been, on this page you talk about the dangers of reconstruction, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's hear the transcript pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Again, the full answer commences on page 43, line 20 through 25 on that page, and then proceeds on page 44 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because that page number is not matching with the ones we have in our computers. Start reading out those part. We can find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It starts with the Professor's answer: "No, not necessarily. That's why I try to explain. You need to know a lot more about the situation. If I'm told you will be examined by the Prosecutor Mr. Nicholls, well, there's one person examining me, so I don't need to know your name. I just assume that that is a Mr. Nicholls, and I don't have to remember the name."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Now I understand the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then he proceeds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then if I could just read the sentence immediately before the word, and it states: "So it depends on the situation. If this person is sent to a certain place where someone is in charge, he needs to find the person in charge as it goes in the army, and if there's someone else who is the highest rank, you go to that person. In his recollection later on, but that's already --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you. "But that's already -- that's why I'm saying this, the danger is that he is now reconstructing that he was sent to meet certain Mr. Beara, whereas in fact he was just looking for the highest in rank or the only colonel." And it proceeds, but that's the end of the quote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I understand your question. May I answer it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may in one second. I'm told that the official transcript now is actually page 25449, and I apologise for not having that earlier. You may, Professor.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reconstruction means that after an event we either get new information about the event or we rethink the event and come to certain conclusions and then enter these conclusions or this new information into our previous memories where they become an indistinguishable part of those memories so that later on when we try again to remember that event we will also remember the details that actually we had not experienced but have added later on. Our research generally shows that what we call the effect of post-event information is that it is inserted in your memories and that people cannot make the distinction between the original memory and the things that were added. So a witness would be totally honest in this example if he replied, I remember that I was told to find Mr. Beara, if -- and I'm only saying if. I'm not saying that it happened in such a way just to get away from the confusions that are entered all the time in this court. I'm not saying that I know what happened. I'm only saying that there's another possibility. That possibility is that this person was sent to meet the colonel or to deliver a message to a group of people, which would make him go to the highest in rank if is he a proper military person, then later on if he was told, well, it was Mr. Beara, that in the end he remembers I was told to tell Mr. Beara so and so, and would in no way be able to make the distinction if questioned about it between what he actually was said and what he now remembers he was told. I'm not proposing this as a factual description of what happened. I'm proposing that as a thing that can happen in memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the concept, sir, of post-event reconstruction? Have you heard of that, by a third person or by another party?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So one possibility is that other people present to you a different -- a different account of the facts that happened, and when they tell you about this, that this might work in your own memory as post-event information and is integrated in your own memory after which you forget the source from which this information actually has come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, help me understand this. How are we to determine whether that information came from the initial source or it was a source from this post-event reconstruction by a third party?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no way you can determine that, at least not by asking the witness because the witness would be unaware of what happened in his memory. The only thing that you can verify is whether there was an opportunity for post-event information, whether he talked to anyone about these events. That is something you can ask a witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me give you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we're now verging into the area, again, of pure speculation. The professor can discuss these topics, which he's an expert on, but having said he can't in any way tie it to any fact in this case, and to my recollection this post-event reconstruction was never put to any witness. It hasn't been put in the trial. It's just now an interesting topic, but it has no connection to this case because any witness in any case is what we're talking about with memory, and I think that's something that is squarely within your ambit and that this is not helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thought Mr. Ostojic was moving on to another topic, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would -- respectfully, I think the Prosecution is wrong, and if the Court permits me to put the next question, although I'd like to put it as a factual matter, although they are allowed to raise hypothetical questions, I'll do so in a hypothetical matter, but specifically with this witness Mr. Milosevic I think we heard testimony in this court from his commander who also testified. If the Court remembers, that commander and Mr. Milosevic actually drove in a car together for approximately two hours and gave the interview on the exact the same day and spoke about the facts upon which they were asked to be interviewed on by the Prosecution. So I dare say that post-event reconstruction by third parties is not in this case. Those were my specific questions at that time, and I think without summarising that evidence, we can refer to it quite plainly as to what both witnesses said in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the question raised by Mr. Nicholls is how it arises out of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Two ways. One, the professor mentions the dangers of reconstruction; two, my learned friend was asking questions specifically about Mr. Milosevic yesterday, and he specifically asked questions both with name retention, which I think impacts on this concept, and he also asked some specific questions when it relates to exposure time and the qualifications in connection with that. It's right on point, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see first how the -- your question would be formulated. Put your question, and we'll see later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hypothetically, Professor, when dealing with Mr. Milosevic in this case and when he is going to his first interview on the 14th of March, 2002, I believe, if he goes with his commander in the same vehicle and drives for approximately an hour and a half to two-plus hours knowing that both are being interviewed by the Office of the Prosecution, what impact, if any, does post-event reconstruction have if the two of them discuss the reason they're going to the Office of the Prosecution as well as the facts upon which each we're going to testify to? But the Court should instruct you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, speaking for myself, the professor would not be a position whether they discussed the matter or not, and he can only answer the question hypothetically and which answer -- in Chamber's view, he gave his answer already in previous. utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer that question, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just want to be certain. Of course, I'm not to judge practical problems. As I remember Mr. Nicholls explaining yesterday, one requirement is, of course, that you have a photo. utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, approximately three and a half years later on July of 1999, they again have an interview with Mr. Egbers; and at that time, sir, they did not conduct a photo board lineup. utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, it has the same disadvantage that you miss an opportunity; although, of course, it must be stated that the longer retention interval, as we call it, the longer the period that has passed, the more likely it becomes that a good witness who understands the rules and who would not guess at a photo board would in the end say, I'm sorry, I'm not certain that I recognise one, and therefore indicate no one, which does not mean that the accused is not present. It only means the witness is not certain enough that he remembers. The likelihood of that happening increases with the retention interval, and therefore, a photo board preferably is administered at the earliest opportunity. Now, not having done it in 1995, then 1999 is the next best, and even, say, a couple years later would be the next best until the moment that pictures of the accused are -- have appeared on billboards everywhere and could have been seen by this witness Egbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So am I correct that your answer would be the same with respect to their third interview with Mr. Egbers in 2000, which was two and a half years prior to the poster boards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object because, again, he's asking these questions now about things that he never put to our investigator, Tomasc Blasczyk who he cross-examined far beyond the question that he came to testify about, which the Drina corps collection. utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, help us understand this theory or concept of wanted posters if you will, Professor, and I asked you a question yesterday, and I apologise because it may have been somewhat awkward. Are you suggesting that if wanted posters are published, that at that point no witnesses thereafter should be given a photo board identification test?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not exactly what I said. I said two things, if I remember correctly. One is that it's very unfortunate to publish posters if there are still witnesses known to you who can be tested in an identification test because in that situation, of course, you should first administer the tests and then publish the posters because if you publish the posters in an area where these witnesses can see them, then it, in my opinion, would not be helpful anymore to test them in a photo board. But if there are witnesses about whom you can decide that they simply had no opportunity to see these photo boards, for instance, because they live in the country where they could never see them, that would make a change. So to give you an example, if the photo boards are published in the former Yugoslavia and you want to test members of DutchBat who live in the Netherlands and who have never returned to Yugoslavia, then there's in principle not so much objection against testing these members of DutchBat. So it's not the general rule. It all depends on whether there is a possibility for witnesses to really have seen them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree that it would be helpful if the investigator or anyone would ask that question to witnesses?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I won't agree to that. As I explained yesterday, if witnesses say, yes, I've seen the boards, that's helpful. Then you know it. But if they say, no, I have not seen them, you must still assume that they might have seen them but don't remember. So irrespective of the answer, you must assume they've seen them, so it's an unnecessary question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And help me understand on page 23 in yesterday's transcript, you were talking about this with my learned friend, and I think they gave an explanation about leads that, you know, one of the reasons purportedly an investigator wouldn't show photographs or showed a lot of photographs to the witness Babic that we were dealing with. That was one of their explanations, the -- that they're looking for leads. And then you talked about this, and it states on page 16, and again, I will get the correct transcript page for the Court. And you say: "And I'm always surprised if I say how easily and how quickly during early investigation stages photographs are shown to witnesses without the realisation that that way you lost the witnesses for later identification purposes, which is not a problem if you have lots and lots of witnesses but which can be very problematic if there is a scarcity of witnesses. And that is why I always recommend that you show photographs to witnesses in order to find a lead if you are desperate because there's no other way of getting leads." I don't fully, with all due respect, understand your answer, so can you help me understand it better?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. What I said is the following: There are two ways in which you can use witnesses' reactions to photos. One is in the investigation period where witnesses looking at photos can give you leads. For instance, a very clear example is you have a photograph of something related to the crime, but you don't know who these people are. In that case, you could ask a witness who is supposed to be familiar with these people to give you the names. That's during investigation. That is what Mr. Nicholls called in order to get a lead. A second use is photo identification. That is where a witness made a statement about things he experienced and remembers, and there is a need to back up this statement by a test that verifies that the witness really met the person or persons he is describing. That's something entirely different. There, the use of photographs in a photo board will be to serve as evidence. Now, in my earlier publications, and I may refer you to the book I wrote about the case of Ivan Demjanjuk where I very carefully explained that, photographs that serve to obtain a lead do not have to conform to any model or prescription. But the outcome of that procedure cannot be used instead of a photo board identification. So the witnesses who looked at photos not conforming to the model of a photo identification board can be helpful to provide leads but cannot later on also be tested in photo boards featuring the same people because if they identify someone in a photo board, that might be because they saw that person in a photograph shown to them and not because they saw that person at the scene of the crime. So there must be no confusion, also, in the mind of investigators between showing photos in order to get a lead and showing photos in order to get evidence from the witness that he really is -- has seen a certain person. And my objection that I noted in my report is -- my objection, my warning, rather, is that in this case some witnesses were shown photographs that did not conform to the model of lineups and that, therefore, the Court must be warned that their responses to those photographs should be interpreted as witnesses giving leads but not as witnesses proving that they actually met someone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just a follow-up question on that because I was really also looking for you to quantify for me where you say lots and lots of witnesses, and then you compare it to a scarcity of witnesses. Can you help me with that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely, and I've seen many cases where you had a variety. If you have a case on which I published, a case of a murder in a bar with 82 witnesses, you may easily use 5 or 10 of those witnesses to give you leads, whom you could show photographs; then you still have 72 witnesses remaining. If, on the other hand, as I had in a supermarket murder, only two witnesses of a brutal murder, and you show both witnesses just photographs of suspects - not in lineups, just single photographs - I would call that disastrous because maybe these witnesses remember the killers very well, but their identification in a photo lineup cannot be used. You lost important evidence, and in that case their entire case might be lost. So my recommendation would be, always keep the minimum number of witnesses that you will need in order to prove identity, and it's not for me which number of witnesses -- to decide which number of witnesses is convincing. I think it's the first -- in the first place the task of the Prosecution to determine which number of identification witnesses they will present as sufficient evidence. It's always wise to keep that minimum number out of the procedure of showing photographs in order to get leads. And if you need three witnesses to prove identity and you've got only three, then you cannot show those three photographs in order to get leads. If you still do that, then you lose your identification witnesses, and that's why I said that sacrifice, the cost of that is high. So that's why I said if you still do that, you must be desperate for getting leads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My first comment I'd like to make concerning what my colleague just said regarding expert witnesses. I refer the Court back to the testimony of witness Butler who was labelled as an expert by the Prosecution and accepted by the Trial Chamber even though there was no possibility to even find out the material that this witness had consulted before making both his report and his testimony. For my colleague to say today that unless you have the whole universe you cannot accept or judge on the expert report is simply astounding. But I simply at this point in time join the objection

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, when the professor was cross-examined and re-examined, whenever these documents were used or referred to, the relevant parts were read into the transcript. There is no need to come back and put all this material in even if it is for the purpose of highlighting the context of the report of the professor. We simply move that should the Court in assessing the report of the professor at a later time feel the need to see these documents, then, of course, the Court -- it will be open to the Court to do so. But for the Prosecution to at this time move to have all these documents admitted would not be the wise thing to do at this time. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may add, since in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- Madam Fauveau and Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, you are the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There are two principles, I think, here, although we're using obviously strong words like "amazing" and -- this Court has set a precedent in this case. We've dealt with each Prosecution witness in a manner, if you're going to use the statement, the Court said we don't need that; we want to judge this case from the witness stand based on the public testimony that we've heard. The Prosecution diligently went through each of those, and we provided it to them. They diligently went throughout transcripts or the interviews that they wished to highlight to, as my learned friend says, found some mistakes or errors in the report of Professor Wagenaar, which he conceded. The danger in setting the precedent now is that I will orally immediately ask this Court to provide me with the universe of all the documents their experts reviewed. A quick example that comes to mind is Kathleen [sic] Barr that we all experienced. She didn't provide us -- they didn't provide us with her entire file nor her notes. During her testimony, the Court allowed on my motion to obtain that documentation. We got it, but we didn't get her entire universe because they complained that it's either privileged or that there's a work product doctrine. It's a poor precedent to set. And the second principle is as to fairness. The Prosecution had the entire binder, has had the report for months. We were always willing to allow them to meet with Professor Wagenaar. At each request they made, we told them in the affirmative they can meet with him. They have had all these interview statements before. To now produce all the interview statements would then allow us to give this Court the entire electronic disclosure filings, and our jobs would then become meaningless. Their jobs would become meaningless. We're then inviting this Court to just take the documentation and just review it on your own without any arguments or cross-examination or direct examination from counsel. I strongly urge that this Court doesn't take this unilateral step to impose that the entire file and as specifically the statements that were produced be given in as evidence; and if they do that, they reconsider their prior orders and require an order that the Prosecution give us the complete files that Mr. Butler, Dr. Wright, Dr. -- Ms. Kathleen [sic] Barr and others that have testified before this Court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau, Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have the same objection as regards Exhibit P3694. This is an interview conducted by the OTP with Celanovic. If the Trial Chamber feels that this statement needs to be part of the case file, then I feel that this should only be as a part of Mr. Wagenaar's report and should not have anything to do with the truth it contains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just would like to join to the objection of Mr. Bourgon as to the witness statement and the

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: 3662, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is not the same as just any other witness, the practice where we haven't put in the whole documentation and we only go through the parts read out. This is an expert report. With Butler's report, Butler exhaustively footnoted his report. All the documents that are footnoted were provided. I think they're hyperlinked so they can click on them. With Kate Barr everything that was asked for was provided. They were provided with her notes. The fact that I could have met with Dr. Wagenaar, the fact that I've cross-examined him for three hours and I tried to do it as quickly as I can, it's impossible -- the alternative is I cross-examine him for weeks and go through each statement because it's important to see not just what he cited but what he didn't cite, and I tried to point that out. I mean, this is very simple, I think. He's got witness summaries that he prepared from reviewing those binders. In the witness summaries, he cites to the parts that he found relevant. Now, it's also important, as I say, what he didn't cite to, and it is; it's just astounding to me that the material that we know was used in his report that he reviewed, the 12 witnesses that they called him to testify about, that they don't want you to be able to see it, to see whether his report was accurate. That doesn't remove our role. That just obscures the basic principle, that footnotes to a report, the documents used in a report are available. That's why they're made available to me so that I can check. I can't think of any reason why you should not be able to have that same ability to check his cites, to read what he says as you would with the Butler report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, before you sit down. Sorry, I just have a question. With reference to 3662, 3694, and 3705, I'm assuming that those three statements are, again, duplicates and overlap with the -- a bundle of documents that you're proposing in your last entry, which is the three binders. Is that correct? These are all statements that were provided to Dr. Wagenaar?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Let me just quickly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: I just wanted to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if you could answer, Mr. Nicholls, whether it would not be sufficient by including those part in the transcript pages by reading out those part?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, I don't think it would, Your Honour, because this is three volumes of material. What I tried to do in my cross-examination was keep it to three hours. I tried to make it shorter, but it was about three hours and 15 minutes, and I was hitting the highlights. I mean, I felt like part of what I was doing was correcting some of his homework and pointing out issues. One, there are very likely in the time I had available points that I missed that may be relevant that then would not be available to you; and there are points that, frankly, I thought may have been important, but I did not try to catch every single issue with every single one of these 12 witnesses in the three hours that I had available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I take it there's no other objections in relation to other documents to be tendered from the Beara Defence or Gvero Defence? Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We would also add before they - I'm sorry, if I can - additional documents that may not have made it on the list, and that would be - but I think we have it in there - the portion of the statement that we looked at with respect to Zoran Malinic. And also, the -- I wanted to use, but I don't think we have --the Court has the OTP 65 ter summary of Zoran Malinic, which we've identified as 2D606.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have a 65 ter number of Malinic's interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. I have it as P3621, but I may have to double-check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. For Mr. Beara's exhibits, I object to -- if this is a proper time or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, let's deal with the submissions, and we'll come back with a decision, hopefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I object to 2D603, the information report, which my friend kept trying to question the witness about unsuccessfully. 2D606, the 65 ter summary, again, that did not -- was not used with the witness and in my view is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the 3621?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know what it is. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Malinic's interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He wants that interview in? I don't object to that interview -- I do object to that interview coming in. There was no questions on that because they were inappropriate, and it wasn't part of his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was it not put to the witness at the last moment? 2D606 is a summary of Zoran Malinic, and 3621 is his interview. Am I correct, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is, but I think on page 41, specifically line 16 through 19, I'm requesting the pertinent pages or that one page that we looked at. There's no need, in my view, for the entirety of the statement as was our practice before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't remember, but I thought that my objection was upheld with the question about Malinic so that it's irrelevant. And that just reminds me, that's the problem with putting in just pages. The Bircakovic interview is a good example because Professor Wagenaar in my submission was possibly mixing up slightly these three different events of -- that are spoken about in the interview he used, and there were other parts of that interview that he looked at that I believe contributed to his confusion about whether the identification is the school in Orahovac, the Zvornik brigade headquarters, or the meeting between Drago Nikolic, Beara, and Popovic. And the only way to unpack that is to see the interview, and that was part of the testimony, and it can't be done by just looking at isolated parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just briefly and ever so briefly, if I may, it's very different if they call the witness and the Court has heard evidence from those witnesses. We have heard evidence from those witnesses. With respect to Mr. Malinic, the Prosecution had him on a 65 ter list and then withdrew him as a witness. We don't know with any certainty if he is going to appear. I think that portion of that statement is consistent with what the Court has done. To argue that now we should have (redacted) (redacted) were used by counsel when appropriate during both direct and cross-examination. They could have been elicited in the testimony. The Court considered that in the full testimony of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Last point, I'm sorry. Nobody yet has pointed today any harm at all that would flow from the Court having available to it this material if it wants to check the cites and check the conclusions of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I submit there is harm. The harm is just bunging this case up with a huge amount of documentation. Having said that, if the Chamber was to find the material helpful, then we on behalf of General Gvero who are not basically involved in this matter would have no objection to it being admitted so long as it's admitted not out of the truth of its contents. Excuse the double negative. I've only, actually, risen not to really deal with that but to deal with our own exhibits. Could I put one thing on the record, please, Your Honour, and that's this: 6D308 on our schedule was in fact page 11 of 2D590, and we're only seeking to have page 11 of that report admitted, and so we've given it a different 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, we, of course, don't want to be left out of this discussion. We agree with the statement of principle by the Gvero Defence, but one practical matter to bring to your attention: If you do bring all of these statements into evidence, there is the possibility that some of us might attempt to cite to those documents in their final briefs for the truth of their contents. Now, as long as -- if these documents are brought in, that does open the possibility of extensive motions to strike and complex submissions about the precise circumstances in which such documents were referred to. So I would just implore the Chamber in any ruling it makes to be clear as to whether the documents are coming in for the truth of their contents or purely to illuminate what was said by the witness on the stand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to add that the part of this transcript requires redaction because Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That has been already taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We come back to the issue and give our ruling after the next break because we need to check some things with our transcript. Shall we bring in the next witness. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, just very briefly on what I consider to be a policy matter related to this. I just wanted the Trial Chamber to know that when this material that we're offering into evidence and other materials, it is not our intention to ever have this material limited to you in the sense of only for the truth of the matter asserted. We think that fine, of course, for you to do that if you feel necessary or any way else you want to treat this, but this material, we would not endorse any restrictions on it except that you use it however or as little as you see fit. That's basically our policy on that, and I just wanted to make that clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a bit different position taken by Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I just wanted to clear that up, and that's why I spoke, so that is our position. We're fine if that's the way you wanted to take it, but I do not want to be part of a limitation partly because of the things that were pointed out by the Borovcanin team. I think that puts you in a difficult position with an old adversarial concept that I think we should just forget.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll consider your position, well, to have postpone our ruling. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, since I was specifically referred to, I think I ought to respond. The difficulty here, speaking very practically, is if one of these documents that goes in, we have no problem with the document being used in order to explain what the witness said on the stand. The problem that's going to arise is if a page in one of these prior statements winds up in a final brief and we don't notice it or if we do notice it, we file a motion to strike, or if the Chamber doesn't notice it, and it winds up as a basis for a conviction in a judgement, that's highly prejudicial. It adds a complexity, and it adds -- in our view undermines the whole process of these proceedings. So furthermore, you have access to all of these documents on e-court. It doesn't need to be become an exhibit in order for you to have a look at it. You can have a look at it without it becoming an exhibit. That's the -- there is a useful purpose for having a distinction between marked for identification and something entered as an exhibit, which presumptively becomes evidence that you can safely rely on in reaching your findings in the judgement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly. It's not all in e-court. That's the -- part of the point. It's not all in e-court; and secondly, I don't see any -- I have a hard time seeing problems in final briefs or judgements since presumably everything will be cited with its exhibit number and will be very easy to trace what came in when through whom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As a practical matter, what's the destiny of an evidence that was tendered but not admitted? That still stays on and the Judges have access to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. All I was going to say -- now is not the time to debate it, but with respect I'm not sure I agree with Mr. Gosnell. It's a difficult issue, and it may be one that we should examine either orally or in writing in due course. So far as Your Honour's question is concerned, I do not know the answer. I don't know whether anyone else can help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that -- back to the issue after the next break. Let's bring in the next witness. I take it to be Mr. Bienenfeld.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. If you could take a solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. AS you know, my name is John Ostojic, and I'm one of the attorneys who represents Mr. Ljubisa Beara. Can you for the record give us your full name?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: My name is Jakov Bienenfeld.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bienenfeld, can you share with us a little bit about your background? What's the highest level of education that you've attained?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: I have an associate university degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May we have your date of birth, please, and your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: [In English] 28 of July, '48, Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know you do speak English. Just so that there's no confusion, may I ask in which language you would prefer to provide answers to some of my questions?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to be sure, I would like to do it in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so I'm clear, can you tell us your ethnic background, and I apologise for asking.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: No problem. I was born in Zagreb. I'm a citizen of Croatia, of the former Yugoslavia first and then Croatia, and my ethnicity is Jewish.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think the record says your ethnicity is Jewish as well as your religion, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: [In English] It's a mistake. Ethnically, ethnically I'm -- [Interpretation] The situation is different in Croatia now. I'm a citizen of Croatia, and my religion is Jewish.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, just share -- thank you. Share with us briefly whether or not you were gainfully employed prior to the war in former Yugoslavia in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: I have my own private company. I've had it for 30 years now. I had it in the former Yugoslavia, and I still have it now in the state of Croatia. I am engaged in the development of software, and as of recently I have also been engaged in construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Turning our attention to the period approximately of 1990 through 1995, can you tell us what you did at that point, if anything, with respect to evacuation of certain population?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: Very well. In early 1990, as you know, an attack was carried out. A bomb was planted on the building of the Jewish community in Zagreb. Immediately after that, I was appointed the head of security of the Jewish community in Zagreb. In keeping with that and in keeping with the duties that that entailed, I handed my company over to my son, and I took care of the Jewish community in the period between 1990 and 1995. According to my free estimate, I concluded that I as a representative of the Jewish national minority had a very good and very suitable environment for all the warring parties to accept me as a neutral, non-religious person who could not fall into the trap of ethnicity or religion, and I realised that I could help in the exchange of the prisoners, and this is what I actually did most of the time. I was involved in the exchange of prisoners between the then-JNA and the Croatian army. During that period of time, I believe that it was already 1991, and when I say that, I don't think I'm mistaken. There were already problems in Bosnia, and we were invited by the community in Sarajevo to launch an initiative for assistance in food, medicines, and to see whether there were any possibilities to launch an initiative to evacuate some members of the Jewish community in the BiH who wanted to be evacuated, and this is what I did and the activities that I was involved in up to 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so that we may obtain a proper parameter, you mentioned that in early 1990 you were head of security of the Jewish community in Zagreb. For how long did you maintain that position?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: Too long. Until 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us, if you will, and I know you mentioned the exchange of POWs, whether or not you were involved in the evacuation of civilian population during the period in which you were chief -- or head of security of the Zagreb Jewish community?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: Look, I've already said that I'm not burdened by any religious affiliation, and I really don't make any difference among people based on their religion. We assisted the evacuation of part of the Jewish community from Sarajevo. I would like to draw attention to a very important detail. I personally evacuated seven convoys, and in every of these convoys members of the Jewish community were always a minority of each and every of these convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're getting a little ahead of ourselves, I think, but let me focus because I wasn't sure if I understood it. You are specifically relating to an evacuation that you participated in in Sarajevo, correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: It did not occur. It was not just a one-off occurrence. It kept on repeating in 1992, 1993, and even maybe 1994. I may be mistaken, but it was a long time ago, and my memory is fading due to age.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me if your organisation of which you were the head of security, whether they had any affiliates that they worked with during that time period?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: To be absolutely precise, I would like to say that the initiative for the evacuation of Jews from Sarajevo was not an initiative of the Jewish community of Zagreb, but the American institution, Joint Distribution Committee, similar to Caritas, who received a query in Sarajevo and launched the operation. And since in Zagreb we had the best logistics and the best equipment, we together with them became involved in the complete operation. As a Jewish community, we participated in the exchange of prisoners between the former Yugoslavia and Croatia on our own, but when it comes to Sarajevo we were partners with the American institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think you mentioned an organisation called Joint, J-O-I-N-T, but I think -- and you correct me if I'm wrong, I think it's referenced from time to time as the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: [In English] Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: Yeah, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, can you describe the events leading up to this evacuation from the population in Sarajevo that you referenced earlier today? How did it come about?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, the war started in Slovenia and then spilled over to Croatia, and then everybody who wanted to see that could see that Bosnia as the ethnically most-divided republic of the former Yugoslavia will also hit hardship very soon. We warned our community in Sarajevo about that, but as in '45, the Jews did not believe what would happen to them. The same situation repeated in Sarajevo in 1991. They did not believe that things might go wrong. When the Croats struck Bosnia, there was a shortage of food and medicine, and they turned to us for help. Actually, they first turned to Joint headquartered in Paris. Joint contacted us. We mounted a radio search in the Jewish community in Sarajevo, and in the Jewish community in Zagreb we ensured communications lines. We started our first food conveys, and after the first convoy when we arrived there, there was a pressure to be evacuated not for the reasons of religious threats but because of the threat of a war. The Jewish community in Sarajevo not for a single moment was threatened as an ethnic community, but there was normal fear among people, and this is actually the first war in the history when we were not threatened as a people. Actually, I would like to point out that everybody treated us with much more respect than could have been expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to focus our attention specifically in connection with the seven convoys that you previously discussed; and in connection with those seven convoys, I think you reference that in each bus there was a minority of Jewish people. Can you tell me what were the other ethnic backgrounds, if you know, of the people that were being evacuated with this 7-convoy evacuation?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: From the point of view of the former Yugoslavia, the composition of these conveys was absolutely multiethnic. There were Serbs, Croats, Jews, the Roma -- or gypsies, as you will. We also had one Albanian. We also had an Afro-American, an African-American. In other words, these were -- these convoys were absolutely multiethnic, but let me explain. You have to understand that Sarajevo - I apologise - that Sarajevo was organised as a ring in the middle. There were Muslims around them, there was a ring of Serbs, and after that there was a ring of Croats on the outer edge. And effectively, every ethnic group had to pass through an enemy territory. For Serbs in Sarajevo to reach Serbs in Pale or Lukovic I had to pass through a Muslim barrier. The Croats in Sarajevo had to pass through both barriers, both Muslim and Serbs. People wondered why Serbs in convoy, why not Serbs were in Sarajevo. That was under the control of Muslims at that moment, and they found it very difficult to get to the Serb territories of Lukovic and Pale, and that's why they found themselves in our convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm still not clear based on the transcript as to the composition of the different ethnic groups. I know you said all of them, but let me put a direct question to you. Within this convoy, this 7-convoy evacuation, were there Bosniaks and/or Bosnian Muslims that were also being evacuated by your organisation and your assistance?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: Look, in Bosnia, the Jewish community numbered some 900 people. It was a very small community, and it could not provide for a normal life such as a community would have. That's why there were interethnic marriages, and this resulted in the fact that over 60 percent of the members of the Jewish community of some -- Sarajevo were married to a non-Jewish person, be it a Muslim, a Croat, or a Serb. However, from my perspective, somebody whose wife is Jewish or whose husband is Jewish at the moment of such a tragedy that prevailed in Sarajevo, there was absolutely no difference between Jews and others, everybody who wanted to leave Sarajevo, and you were limited by numbers. It was not an organisation to export or import people into and out of Bosnia. If you wanted to smuggle somebody, to put it that way, you had to invent their origin. You had to give him or her a story so as to make the Bosnian authorities provide him or her with documents that would allow them to leave the territory of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Prior to the completion of the evacuation - specifically, I'm referencing to these seven convoys - did you have an opportunity or did you negotiate with the various ethnic groups? I think you mentioned you did because you had to pass through the different areas, so if you could just clarify that for me.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: I arrived from Croatia, and Croatia had the administrative control of the HVO, the Croatian Defence counsel, and it's a notorious fact. When we went there, we did not have to have any licences. However, when we wanted to pass through the Muslim or Serbian territories, this required a lot of negotiations, but all these were -- proved to be successful at the end. The then-head of the counterintelligence, General Vasiljevic, referred us to General Milovanovic as a person with whom we could negotiate. At that moment, he was the Chief of Staff or something to that effect, and we negotiated with him about all the convoys that were supposed to cross the territory. In Bosnia, we negotiated with Bosniaks, and this was done between the Jewish community of Sarajevo and somebody whose name I can't remember. The name escapes me. He was the vice-president of the Presidency. If I remember, I'll tell you. And we did not have any problems with these negotiations. I repeat once again, this is the only thing that I would like to repeat and something that people have to be given credit for, and that is that from all the three ethnic groups we received maximum support when it came to the evacuation of the members of our Jewish community of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name --

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: Name was Ganic. [Interpretation] Family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have an opportunity to meet or are you familiar with the name of Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the name, and I met with Mr. Beara. I met him when we were negotiating the passage of the second convoy. There was a meeting which I attended together with General Milovanovic, and I was escorted by the appropriate services of the Croatian Defence counsel. We had been invited to that meeting with General Milovanovic, and Mr. Beara was also present at the meeting as the head or chief of the counterintelligence of the then-Army of Republika Srpska. He attended our negotiations for the organisation of the second convoy. Actually, the way I saw it was that we were kind of transferred under his competence for safety reason, and that is -- that was the only time when I met him tete-a-tete and when I had an opportunity to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, and we'll get into the some of the details of that. But first, if you can tell me to the best of your recollection, what year or what month did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: Well, you're asking quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: It may have been late spring 1992, I think, but I could not swear that this is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Where did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: At Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You referenced other -- or you mentioned a couple other individuals. To the best of your recollection, can you give us a more detailed description as to how many people participated in these negotiations with respect to the seven convoys as you've referenced it, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: [In English] You think on this meeting or generally?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In particular this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: [In English] This meeting was present General Milovanovic, [Interpretation] Mr. Beara, Mr. Zarko Keza, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how long did the meeting last?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: [In English] one hour, one hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, what occurred which necessitated this meeting with, among others, Mr. Beara in Pale? Was there a problem with the first convoy?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personally, I believe - this is just my speculation - that Mr. Beara had been invited to attend the meeting only because we had announced that that convoy would not be unique, a one-off occurrence, that is, that we intended to make several journeys and bring food to Sarajevo. This was a delicate issue, and I believe that he as a professional occupying that position had been given a task to look at the whole situation from his professional point of view and to provide us with an unhindered and relatively clear passage as I've already told you. I was escorted by the member of the -- appropriate member the HVO, which was also in charge of securing our passage to the boarder, and it was only natural for me to see his counterpart, the gentleman in question, attending that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned "unhindered and relatively clear passage." Was that accomplished with respect to the evacuation process that was undergoing in Sarajevo that you referenced?

utterances.speaker: JAKOV BIENENFELD
utterances.text: Except for one isolated case when because of the circumstances of its size the convoy had to be divided into two so that one of my colleagues pulled one of the convoys out, and the other one stayed in Sarajevo, and I came out with that one six hours later. A group of people, according to information which was accessible to me later, a group of people in uniforms entered the bus, confiscated money, gold from the passengers. When I was informed about that, I felt very bad about that, not only because of the valuables because that was the entire property those people owned on the bus. I was very angry about it and indignant, and I called General Milovanovic first, and I must admit I said all sorts of things to him, and the comment to that was that I wanted to secure the return of all of those things with the utmost speed, and I -- and now this is the first time since the war that this was said publicly. General Milovanovic understood the seriousness of that problem, and that was something that -- it could not at that point be of any use politically or in other -- any other way to Republika Srpska. At the time, he said that he would assign that to Beara. I said, I don't care who he entrusted that task to, as long as it was resolved, and I must say that this was in the evening on the next day in the morning. At the crossing, Zarko picked up a sack, which was definitely to the last penny all of the property that was confiscated. There was one small coin missing, and it was all returned with an apology. We never had anybody hurt in the convoy, and as for the relationships of the Republika Srpska towards the Jewish community and the transference of people of Sarajevo, we always had an ambulance, an escort in the front, an escort in the back with us, and we were absolutely supported in every way in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, after this hour, hour and a half --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.
